caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 41 of 1973
lawyer:
Asrarul Hossain with Abdul Azim ----- For the appellants 
Abdul Hasib with M.A. Tariq ----- For the respondent.
parties:
Pubali Bank Ltd ----- Appellant
Vs.
Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Altaf Hossain, J- This appeal is directed against the Judgment and decree passed, by the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dacca on 31.8.72 in Money Suit No. 10 of 1957. The suit arose out of the following facts:- The plaintiff Corporation entered into a contract with defendant No. 2 where under the plaintiff agreed to purchase from the defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 2 agreed to supply to the plaintiff 2500 L/ tons of potato seeds of Shillong variety. It was agreed that the, defendant No.2 will deliver 1000 L/tons by 20.10.62 and 1500 L/tons by 31.10.62. The defendant No. 2 furnished a Bank guarantee from defendant No. 1 Bank for satisfactory performance of the contract. Under the guarantee, the defendant No.1 Bank undertook to pay unconditionally on demand a sum equal to 10% of the total value of the goods amounting to Rupees 1,53,125/- without any further question and without reference to the contractor (defendant No. 2). It. was stipulated that the guarantee would remain in force till the date of due completion of the contract and final adjustment of accounts or till 30.11.62 whichever date was later. The defendant No. 2 failed to effect supply within the stipulated delivery dates and on the request of the defendant No. 2 the plaintiff Corporation extended time for delivery of the 1000 L/tons of potato seeds till 30.10.62 and of the 1500 L/tons of potato seeds till 15.11.62. In spite of the extension of time, the defendant No. 2 defaulted in delivering the first installment of seeds and supplied to the Corporation only 5621 L/tons of the seeds within 30.10.62, the extended date of delivery. The balance 4371 L/tons was not delivered. The Corporation thereupon called upon the Bank to credit the guaranteed amount to its account on 24.11.62 but the Bank refused to do so. Subsequent demand of the plaintiff upon the Bank to encase the guarantee was also of no effect. The plaintiff also repeatedly demanded of the contraction defendant No. 2 to pay liquidated damages and other sums payable under the contract, but the defendant No. 2 also failed to meet the demand. The plaintiff there-upon filed the suit. The defendant No. 2 entered appearance but did not ultimately turn up to contest the suit. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that o 9.41.62 plaintiff Corporation decided that they .would not require the balance quantity of .43½ L/tons of paddy seeds and so there could not be any question of non-performance of the contract, that  the Government of India declared a State of Emergency on 20.10.62 and the defendant No. 2 could not supply the balance quantity of the seeds due to circumstances beyond his control and that the defendant had already performed 82% of the contract and the remaining 18% could not be performed. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence adduced in the case held, negativing all the contentions of the defence, that the defence plea of the defendant No. 2's failure to supply the balance quantity due to circumstances beyond his control could not be accepted that the defence story that the plaintiff had decided that they would not require the balance is false and that since the defendant No. 2 undertook to make an unconditional payment of Rs. 1,53,125/00 to the plaintiff on demand without any further question and reference to the contractor the plaintiff was legally entitled to realise the amount of the guarantee from the defendant No.1. On the above findings the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit directing that the plaintiff do realise Rs. 1,5 .125/00 from the defendant No. 1. Being aggrieved, the defendant No. 1 bus preferred this appeal. 

 6. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant Bank, submits that in the unreported decisions the Appellate Division was concerned with the question whether temporary injunction should be granted or not and they have held that temporary injunction should not be granted considering the question of balance of convenience. We have carefully gone through the decisions. The appellate Division has in these cases, no doubt, considered the question of balance of convenience but that was not only question with which it concerned itself.' It has also examined the nature of obligation of the Bank created by the bank guarantee and indicated the character of a Bank guarantee qua the contract of purchase and supply. The Appellate Division has clearly indicated that though the contract of guarantee between the purchaser and the bank is ancillary to the contract between the put chaser and the supplier yet it is independent of it. The Appellate Division has laid down the proposition that such performance guarantee is not dependent on anything else excepting the buyer making a formal demand alleging failure on the part of the seller to perform the contract in part or in full. The Appellate Division has further observed that if it is made a part of the contract and placed at par with other terms and conditions of the contract, the very purpose of taking performance guarantee by the buyer may be frustrated. When the holder of the guarantee makes a demand, the bank is only obliged to comply with the demand. We are unable to accept the contention of Mr. Asrarul Hossain that the decisions of the Appellate Division in the Civil Appeals relied on by Mr. Hasib do not provide any guidance for a decision of this case. In taking this view we are not unmindful of the fact that in the Bank guarantee Ext. l the commitment for scheduled delivery was noted. Reading the Bank guarantee Ext 1 as a whole, we are of the opinion that the commitment schedule has been shown in the Bank guarantee only by way of reference and the commitment schedule has nothing to do with the terms and condition of the guarantee. The bank has agreed to make an unconditional payment on demand without any further question and without reference to the contractor. The words "without any further question and without reference to the contractor" make it clear that the bank is not to be an arbiter in a dispute between the purchaser and the supplier whether in respect of the performance of the contract or otherwise. On an allegation made by the purchaser that there has been a failure of performance on the part of the supplier, the bank is hound unconditionally to pay the amount on demand. The only condition of the Bank guarantee is that the purchaser should make a demand on the bank and when this has been done, the condition of the guarantee has been fulfilled and the bank is bound to make the payment without any further question and without reference to the contractor. As to what the purchaser is entitled to recover from the supplier as liquidated damages and/or penalty for the default of the supplier is a question between' the purchaser and the supplier. The Bank cannot raise this plea. The question as to what part of the contract has been per-formed by the supplier and what part has not been performed is not also relevant In this view of the matter, we are of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge has taken a correct view of the law in holding that "the defendant No. 1 undertook to make an unconditional payment of Rs. 1,53,125 00 to the plaintiff on demand without any further question and reference to the contractor," and "admittedly the contractor did not perform the contract as per terms agreed upon between the parties" and as such "the plaintiff is legally entitled to realise the amount of the guarantee" and in decreeing the suit.
